name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
question: How do I teach a model a skill or format cheaply?
summary: Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on input–output examples of the behaviour you want. LoRA freezes the original weights and trains small low-rank matrices beside them, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude; QLoRA also stores the frozen weights in 4 bits, so large models fit on a single GPU. The adapter is a small file you can swap per task.
useCases: A consistent format, tone or house style
A narrow task with a few thousand good examples
Shrinking long prompts into the weights at high volume

items.detail: trainable A (r × d) and B (d × r) per adapted matrix; W stays frozen
10,000× fewer trainable parameters and 3× less GPU memory than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B
4-bit NF4 base weights plus LoRA; a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU
about 16 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision
around 1e-4 for adapters versus about 2e-5 for full fine-tuning
completion-only or assistant-only loss, not on the prompt

steps: Collect a few thousand clean, representative examples in chat format
Start with LoRA on all linear layers, rank 8–16, loss on completions only
Use QLoRA if the model does not fit in memory
Hold out an eval set; stop before validation loss rises
pitfalls: Too many epochs on small data: the model memorises and overfits
Training data that disagrees with the prompt you will use in production
No held-out set, so overfitting goes unnoticed
remember: Freeze the model, train a small adapter, hold out a test set.
caption: Trainable parameters for one 4096 × 4096 matrix: full versus LoRA rank 16.

steps.title: Collect reviewed conversations
steps.text: 5,000 real support chats, each checked so the reply follows the four-part format. The model learns exactly what it is shown, errors included.

steps.title: Hold out a test set
steps.text: 10% is set aside and never trained on. Only held-out scores say whether the model learned the format or memorised the examples.

steps.title: Train on the replies only
steps.text: assistant_only_loss computes the loss on the assistant’s turns, so the model learns to answer, not to imitate customers.

steps.title: Add a LoRA adapter
steps.text: The 8B weights stay frozen. Small rank-16 matrices beside every linear layer are trained: about 0.5% of the parameters.

steps.title: Quantise the base (QLoRA)
steps.text: Storing the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 cuts its memory about four times, so training fits on a single 24 GB GPU.

steps.title: Two epochs, then evaluate
steps.text: More passes over 5,000 examples start to overfit. Format compliance on the held-out set rose from 81% to 97%.

goals: See why adapters train a tiny share of parameters

practice.scenario: A payments company wanted support replies in a fixed four-part format and a consistent tone for 1.5 million conversations a month. Prompting reached 81% format compliance on a large model. Supervised fine-tuning of an 8B open model with LoRA on 5,000 reviewed conversations reached 97% compliance on a held-out set. The adapter was 0.5% of the model’s parameters, trained in under three hours on one GPU with QLoRA, and served at a fraction of the cost.

industries.use: Consistent support replies in a fixed format and tone
Clause summaries in a house style reviewers expect
Product descriptions in brand voice for thousands of SKUs

practice.analogy: Adding a specialist attachment to a machine rather than rebuilding the machine: the base stays frozen and a small adapter learns the new job. QLoRA stores the machine compressed so it fits on a smaller bench.

library.name: Hugging Face TRL + PEFT
library.what: SFTTrainer runs supervised fine-tuning; passing a LoraConfig trains a LoRA adapter instead of all the weights.

practice.note: assistant_only_loss trains only on the assistant’s turns. Keep 10% of the data aside and evaluate on it; never tune on the test set.

samples.code:
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

data = load_dataset("json", data_files="support_chats.jsonl")["train"]
split = data.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=7)    # hold out a test set

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(            # QLoRA: 4-bit base
    "your-org/base-8b",
    quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
        bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16))

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(output_dir="sft-support", learning_rate=1e-4,
                   num_train_epochs=2, assistant_only_loss=True),
    train_dataset=split["train"], eval_dataset=split["test"],
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear",
                           task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("sft-support/adapter")

numericDrill.question: LoRA adds two matrices A (r × d) and B (d × r) beside a frozen d × d weight. For d = 4,096 and rank r = 16, how many trainable parameters does one such weight get?
numericDrill.answer: 2 × 4,096 × 16 = 131,072, against 16,777,216 in the frozen matrix: about 0.78%. Across the model, adapters usually total well under 1% of the parameters, which is why they train and store cheaply.

interview.question: How do LoRA and QLoRA differ?
interview.answer: Both freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapters. QLoRA also stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, which cuts memory by roughly four times compared with 16-bit weights, so a 70B model can be tuned on a single 48–80 GB GPU. Quality is usually close to LoRA; training is somewhat slower.

interview.question: How do you know an SFT run has overfitted?
interview.answer: Training loss keeps falling while loss or accuracy on a held-out set stops improving or gets worse, often after too many epochs on a small dataset. Outputs start copying training examples verbatim. Hold out a test set from the start, evaluate every epoch and keep the best checkpoint.

mistakes.mistake: Training three or more epochs on 500 examples
mistakes.fix: Use more data or fewer epochs, and watch held-out loss

mistakes.mistake: Computing loss on the user’s turns too
mistakes.fix: Train only on the assistant’s replies

What does QLoRA add to LoRA?
options: Storing the frozen base in 4-bit precision
quiz.explanation: 4-bit NF4 storage cuts memory about four times.

quiz.question: Training accuracy is 99% and held-out accuracy 73%. What is happening?
options: Data leakage into the test set
quiz.explanation: A big train–test gap means memorisation.

quiz.question: Which practices reduce overfitting in SFT? Select all that apply.
options: Training for ten epochs on 500 examples
quiz.explanation: More data and fewer passes help; the others hide or cause overfitting.

quiz.question: Roughly how much memory does full fine-tuning need per parameter with Adam in mixed precision?
quiz.explanation: Weights, gradients and optimiser states add up to about 16 bytes.

quiz.question: Why is assistant_only_loss (or completion-only loss) useful?
options: It trains only on the replies the model should produce
It removes the need for a test set
quiz.explanation: The model learns to answer, not to imitate users.

quiz.question: The QLoRA paper showed which result?
options: A 65B model tuned on a single 48 GB GPU
quiz.explanation: 4-bit base plus LoRA fitted 65B on one 48 GB GPU.

quiz.question: Adapters on all linear layers versus attention only usually give…
options: Slightly better quality for a few more parameters
quiz.explanation: More modules adapt more of the network at small cost.

quiz.question: Why are LoRA adapters convenient in production?
options: They are small files that can be swapped or merged
They make inference slower by design
quiz.explanation: One base can serve several task adapters.

quiz.question: You have 300 noisy examples. What is the best move before tuning?
options: Clean them and collect more, or improve the prompt
quiz.explanation: Quality and quantity of data matter most.

quiz.question: Which belong in an SFT dataset for a support bot? Select all that apply.
options: Real customer messages with reviewed replies
Replies that follow the target format
quiz.explanation: Test cases stay out of training; real, correct, formatted examples go in.

quiz.question: What does the LoRA rank r control?
options: The size of the adapter’s inner dimension
quiz.explanation: Higher rank, more capacity and more parameters.

quiz.question: The original LoRA paper reported, for GPT-3 175B, trainable parameters reduced by about…
quiz.explanation: About 10,000 times fewer, with 3× less GPU memory.

quiz.question: An 8B model with QLoRA needs roughly how much memory for the 4-bit base weights?
quiz.explanation: About half a byte per parameter plus overheads.

quiz.question: Which is a typical LoRA learning rate compared with full fine-tuning?
quiz.explanation: Adapters usually use higher learning rates.

quiz.question: After SFT, the model follows the new format but general answers got worse. What is this called?
quiz.explanation: Narrow tuning can erode other skills.

quiz.question: When should you merge a LoRA adapter into the base weights?
options: To serve one task with no adapter overhead
quiz.explanation: Merging removes the extra matrix multiply at inference.

quiz.question: How should the held-out set be chosen?

From the training data after training
